To: Engineering Leadership  
From: Infrastructure Engineering  
Subject: Local AI capacity: optimize before expanding  
Date: [date]

This memo recommends that we not purchase additional local AI hardware in the current budget cycle. Instead, we should fund a bounded, instrumented utilization program and reserve the capital as a contingent option. The decision is not a rejection of growth; it is a sequencing choice based on total cost, latency risk, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility.

Our current capacity picture is insufficiently measured. GPU utilization as a single percentage is misleading because it can be high while memory bandwidth, KV-cache capacity, or scheduler queueing are the real constraints. We need per-model tokens per second, prefill and decode latency at p50 and p95, queue wait time, VRAM headroom, batch efficiency, and power draw per useful token. Without those, a purchase decision is likely to add expensive idle capacity or fail to fix a software bottleneck. The utilization program should cover continuous batching, paged KV cache, admission control, model routing, quantization where quality permits, response caching, and multi-model serving. It should also evaluate MIG or time-slicing where isolation matters and autoscaling of local queues where demand is bursty. These changes are software and configuration work; they are cheap to try and easy to reverse.

Cost is the first reason to sequence this way. Additional local hardware carries capex, depreciation, power, cooling, rack space, spares, and staff time. Idle GPUs are not free; they consume budget and attention. Utilization improvements also cost engineering time, but that time is bounded and can be staged. The opportunity cost matters because a small team spending weeks on procurement, drivers, and capacity planning is not improving model quality, evaluation, or product reliability. If the utilization work succeeds, we avoid capex and gain operational headroom. If it fails for genuine capacity reasons, we will have better data for a purchase and a clearer specification.

Latency and reliability cut both ways. Better batching and routing can raise throughput, but aggressive batching can hurt tail latency, so we must define service-level objectives for interactive and batch workloads separately. Utilization gains can also reduce spare capacity, which is exactly what protects reliability during node failure, thermal throttling, driver issues, or unexpected load. We should not consume all headroom. A purchase adds capacity and failure domains, but it also adds operational complexity and may not improve p95 latency if the bottleneck is scheduling or memory. The utilization program should explicitly preserve a reliability margin and test failover under load.

Reversibility favors optimization first. Software and scheduling changes can be rolled back quickly; hardware procurement has lead times, vendor commitments, integration work, and resale risk. Cloud burst capacity can be a reversible pressure valve for peak demand, though it introduces data residency, cost variability, and network latency considerations. We should keep a small contingency budget for rental or cloud burst rather than commit to permanent local capacity before we know the shape of demand.

Our recommendation is therefore to approve a four-to-six week utilization sprint with clear success criteria and a purchase gate. Success means meeting agreed p95 latency and queue-wait targets at forecast peak while retaining a defined reliability margin and staying within power and cost budgets. If those targets are met, defer purchase and revisit at the next planning cycle. If they are not met and the bottleneck is genuinely compute capacity rather than scheduling, memory, or model choice, proceed with a purchase sized from measured demand. We should also set triggers for earlier purchase if a strategic workload has a hard deadline that utilization work cannot meet.

Uncertainty is real. Our workload forecast is noisy, model mix may change, and some utilization gains depend on framework support and team capacity. We should treat the sprint as an experiment with instrumentation, not as an assumption. The recommendation is clear but conditional: optimize and measure first, preserve the option to buy, and buy only when measured demand and reliability requirements justify irreversible capex.

**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** Engineering Leadership  
**From:** Platform Engineering  
**Subject:** Local AI capacity strategy: buy more hardware or improve utilisation

**Recommendation:** Do not commit capital to additional local AI hardware in this budget cycle. Fund a focused utilisation program first, with a capped, pre-approved hardware contingency that triggers only if defined capacity and latency thresholds are crossed after that work. This is not a claim that our current fleet is sufficient indefinitely; it is a claim that we do not yet know whether the bottleneck is capacity or how we schedule, batch, route, and reserve it.

The cost case is asymmetric. Additional local AI hardware carries capital expense, depreciation, rack space, power and cooling, spares, and operational burden, and it begins to cost us the moment it is ordered rather than the moment it is useful. Utilisation work costs engineering time and better observability, but much of it is software and configuration that can be tuned incrementally. If our current utilisation is uneven—some devices saturated while others idle, large models occupying memory for small requests, or batch sizes chosen without regard to tail latency—then buying more hardware risks scaling a scheduling problem rather than solving it. The relevant metric is not average utilisation but useful throughput within latency SLOs at acceptable queue depth, including headroom for failover and maintenance.

Latency and reliability pull in opposite directions from raw utilisation. Aggressive batching and consolidation can raise throughput and reduce idle capacity, but they can also increase p95 and p99 latency, especially under bursty arrival patterns. Over-consolidation reduces redundancy and makes correlated failure more likely; a fleet that looks efficient on average may have no reserve for a node failure, thermal throttling, or a model rollout that temporarily doubles memory pressure. A good utilisation program therefore needs SLO-aware scheduling, preemption, model routing, caching, quantization where quality permits, and explicit reserved headroom rather than a single “maximise utilisation” target. If we can recover meaningful capacity through these measures while preserving tail latency and failover margin, the effective cost per useful request falls without new capex.

Opportunity cost matters in both directions. Engineering weeks spent on scheduling and observability are weeks not spent on product-facing model work, and hardware capital is capital not available for other priorities. But idle or poorly scheduled hardware is also an opportunity cost: it represents paid capacity that is not converting into served requests. The right comparison is the marginal cost of the next reliable, low-latency unit of capacity, whether obtained by utilisation improvements, a small leased burst, or purchased hardware. Hardware procurement has long lead times and poor reversibility; once ordered and racked, it is difficult to unwind without sunk cost and operational disruption. Software scheduling changes are far more reversible, and a lease or short-term burst capacity arrangement preserves optionality while demand forecasts remain uncertain.

Uncertainty is real. We do not yet have a stable picture of arrival rates, model mix, context lengths, acceptable batch delays, or future product demand. Vendor lead times and power constraints add further uncertainty. That argues for a staged decision rather than a binary one. I recommend a six-to-eight week utilisation sprint with clear instrumentation: per-device and per-model utilisation, queue wait time, p95 and p99 latency, memory headroom, failure reserve, and a capacity model that translates workload into required GPU-hours under our SLOs. In parallel, define trigger conditions for the contingency: sustained demand that cannot be met after optimisation, tail latency consistently outside SLO despite scheduling changes, or insufficient failover headroom during peak load. If those conditions are met, buy or lease targeted capacity rather than a broad expansion.

The clear recommendation is therefore to improve utilisation first and treat hardware purchase as a conditional second step. This preserves reversibility, avoids premature capital lock-in, and gives us the data to buy the right capacity if we genuinely need it. The main risk is that utilisation work takes longer than expected or cannot recover enough headroom; the capped contingency and explicit triggers are intended to contain that risk without pretending the uncertainty is resolved.

**MEMORANDUM**

**To:** AI Platform Team  
**From:** Engineering  
**Subject:** Capacity decision: buy more local AI hardware or improve utilisation of existing capacity

We need to decide whether to add local AI hardware or to invest first in getting more useful work out of the hardware we already own. My recommendation is to improve utilisation first through a time-boxed, reversible programme, and to defer additional local purchases until that work demonstrates a sustained compute bottleneck that cannot be resolved more cheaply. This is not a rejection of hardware; it is a sequencing decision. If the pilot shows that queueing and latency remain unacceptable after sensible optimisation, we should buy incremental capacity, preferably in modular or leased form before committing to a large capital purchase.

The cost case is broader than the purchase price of accelerators. Additional local hardware brings power and cooling load, rack space, networking, spares, depreciation, and operational attention. For a small team, the opportunity cost is especially important: every hour spent procuring, installing, and operating new nodes is an hour not spent improving scheduling, batching, model placement, memory efficiency, or failure handling. Utilisation work lowers the marginal cost per request and defers capital expenditure, but it also has an engineering cost and will not scale indefinitely. The comparison should therefore be between the marginal cost of another unit of optimised throughput and the marginal cost of another unit of capacity, including the less visible costs of ownership.

Latency and reliability need to be treated as symptoms before they are treated as capacity shortages. Queue wait is often driven by batching policy, model placement, memory fragmentation, preemption, or poor routing rather than raw compute. More hardware helps when the bottleneck is genuinely compute-bound, but it can add idle capacity and failure surface when the bottleneck is scheduling or memory. Reliability cuts both ways. More nodes increase the number of components that can fail and put more pressure on power and cooling, while better utilisation can create headroom for failover and graceful degradation. Aggressive packing, however, can reduce fault tolerance, so we should preserve explicit headroom for burst traffic and node loss rather than optimising utilisation to the point of fragility.

Opportunity cost and reversibility should shape the decision. A hardware purchase ties up capital and team attention, has procurement lead times, and is only partially reversible through resale or repurposing. Utilisation improvements such as scheduling changes, batching, quantisation, cache management, model routing, tiering, and burst-to-cloud policies are comparatively cheap to try and easy to roll back. They also preserve optionality if workload mix or model sizes change. Cloud burst is not a permanent substitute for local capacity, because it introduces data egress, cost variability, and different latency characteristics, but it is a useful reversible buffer while we gather evidence.

I recommend a four-to-six week utilisation pilot with clear purchase triggers. We should measure queue wait at p95 and p99, accelerator busy time, memory headroom, preemption frequency, error rates, and the proportion of requests that could be served by smaller or cached models. We should implement the highest-leverage scheduling and memory improvements, preserve reliability headroom, and use cloud burst only for clearly bounded overflow. We should buy more local hardware if, after those changes, sustained queue latency still violates service objectives, utilisation is high with memory headroom, and demand forecasts remain robust. We should prefer incremental, modular, or leased capacity first so the decision remains reversible. The main uncertainty is workload forecasting: arrival rates, model sizes, and latency requirements may shift faster than procurement cycles. That uncertainty argues for staged commitments rather than a large upfront purchase. My clear recommendation is therefore to optimise utilisation now, set explicit thresholds for buying later, and keep the first capacity expansion reversible.

**Internal Engineering Memo**

**To:** Engineering Leadership  
**From:** Infrastructure Engineering  
**Subject:** Local AI Capacity: Optimize Before Expanding

The immediate question is whether to buy additional local AI hardware or to invest first in improving utilization of the equipment we already own. The answer is not purely financial, because the two paths differ in latency behavior, failure modes, opportunity cost, and how easily we can undo a bad decision. My recommendation is to fund a focused utilization and scheduling program now, with explicit capacity triggers for procurement, rather than committing capital to new hardware immediately. That recommendation is conditional: if sustained queueing and tail-latency breaches persist after the program has removed obvious inefficiencies, we should buy targeted capacity rather than continue to over-optimize a constrained pool.

The cost case is often misread as a simple comparison between capital expenditure and software effort. Local hardware carries not only purchase price but also depreciation, rack space, power, cooling, firmware and driver maintenance, spare parts, and engineering time to keep a heterogeneous pool healthy. Idle capacity is expensive, but so is a pool that is nominally busy while being inefficient: low effective utilization can hide behind high GPU allocation if memory capacity, KV-cache pressure, or poor batching leaves compute underused. Conversely, utilization work has its own cost, and the team time spent on schedulers, observability, model routing, quantization, caching, and multi-tenancy is real opportunity cost. That effort may delay product work, but it also produces reusable operational leverage and avoids locking capital into a workload forecast that may change.

Latency is the strongest argument for caution about simply adding hardware. More devices can reduce queue depth, but they do not automatically fix tail latency caused by contention, oversized batches, cold starts, or inefficient prefill and decode scheduling. A utilization program can introduce priority classes, admission control, preemption, and workload-aware batching so that interactive requests meet p95 and p99 targets while batch jobs absorb spare capacity. Hardware expansion can help once the remaining latency problem is genuinely capacity-bound, but buying first risks masking scheduling defects and making the system more expensive to operate. We should measure queue wait, time to first token, inter-token latency, and effective memory utilization, not just device occupancy.

Reliability also favors improving the existing pool before expanding it. A larger fleet increases redundancy but also increases failure surface, firmware variance, and maintenance coordination. Utilization improvements can be designed with headroom and failure domains in mind, including drain policies, health checks, and graceful degradation when a node is unavailable. Overcommitting the current pool without such controls would be reckless, so the program must preserve spare capacity for failover and maintenance. If reliability requirements demand geographic or hardware redundancy that a single local pool cannot provide, that is a legitimate reason to procure, but it should be justified by availability targets rather than by average utilization alone.

Opportunity cost and reversibility sharpen the recommendation. Hardware procurement has long lead times, limited configurability, and a sunk-cost character; once bought, the capacity is difficult to resize or repurpose if model architectures or demand shift. Software and process improvements are comparatively reversible: we can tune, roll back, or retire them as evidence accumulates. A staged approach also preserves optionality. We can use cloud burst capacity or short-term vendor commitments for peak demand while the utilization program matures, then buy local hardware only where sustained demand and latency SLOs justify it.

There is genuine uncertainty here. Our demand forecast is noisy, model mix may change quickly, and current utilization metrics may not capture memory-bandwidth or KV-cache bottlenecks. The recommendation is therefore not “never buy,” but “do not buy until we have exhausted reversible improvements and can show a persistent capacity gap.” I propose a defined evaluation window with SLO-based triggers: sustained queueing, repeated tail-latency breaches, or inability to meet reliability headroom after optimization would justify a targeted purchase. Until then, improving utilization is the lower-regret path.

MEMORANDUM

To: Engineering Leadership and Compute Planning Group
From: Infrastructure Engineering
Subject: Local AI compute capacity: buy more hardware or improve utilisation

This memo recommends that we defer additional local AI hardware purchases for at least one quarter and instead fund a focused utilisation program on the fleet we already own. The recommendation is conditional rather than permanent. If the program fails to produce measurable headroom, or if service-level objectives continue to be missed under realistic demand, we should buy capacity. But buying now, before we understand why existing capacity is underused, would convert a reversible software and operations problem into an expensive, slow-to-undo capital decision.

The cost case is straightforward but easy to misread. Additional GPUs carry purchase price, depreciation, power and cooling, rack space, spares, firmware and driver maintenance, and the engineering time required to integrate them into scheduling, monitoring, and incident response. Those costs are real even when the hardware sits idle, and idle capacity is the most expensive kind because it consumes budget and attention without improving throughput. Utilisation work has its own cost, chiefly engineering hours, but it is comparatively small and can be staged. We should measure utilisation at the level that matters: not just GPU allocation, but memory bandwidth, compute occupancy, KV-cache pressure, batch efficiency, and queue wait time by workload class. A fleet can look busy while being inefficient because requests are serialised, models are poorly placed, or pre- and post-processing dominate. Fixing those issues often yields more usable capacity than a marginal hardware purchase.

Latency is the constraint that makes utilisation work non-trivial. Batching and queueing can improve throughput but can also increase tail latency, so the program must be SLO-aware rather than chasing a single utilisation number. We should route interactive requests to latency-sensitive pools, use smaller or quantised models where quality permits, cache common results, apply admission control and preemption where appropriate, and schedule batch work into off-peak windows. The goal is not maximum utilisation; it is predictable latency at acceptable cost. If we buy hardware without this discipline, we risk adding capacity that is similarly misallocated and still missing tail-latency targets.

Reliability also argues for understanding the current fleet before expanding it. More nodes add failure domains, firmware variance, and operational surface area for a small team. Utilisation improvements can improve reliability by adding observability, health checks, graceful draining, and deliberate spare-capacity policies. They can also expose aging hardware or single points of failure that a purchase would mask rather than fix. We need headroom for failover and maintenance, but that headroom should be measured and intentional, not assumed.

The opportunity cost is mostly engineering attention. A small team cannot simultaneously run a deep utilisation program, integrate new hardware, and maintain current services without trading something off. Hardware procurement also has lead times and vendor uncertainty, so it is not a quick fix. Software and scheduling changes are reversible: we can roll them back, adjust thresholds, or redeploy capacity if demand shifts. A hardware purchase is far less reversible, tying up capital and rack space for years. Given uncertain demand forecasts and model-mix changes, reversibility has real value.

My recommendation is therefore to approve a time-boxed utilisation effort with clear owners, instrumentation, and a decision gate. We should define in advance what would trigger a purchase: sustained demand that cannot be met within latency SLOs after utilisation fixes, repeated reliability incidents caused by insufficient headroom, or a forecast that remains robust under conservative assumptions. If those triggers are met, buying is justified. If not, we will have bought ourselves information and headroom at low cost. The uncertainty is genuine, but the asymmetry is clear: improve utilisation first, measure honestly, and keep the purchase option open.
